I've gathered substantial material from the searches and fetched pages. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes from what these sources actually say.

## Mark 10:27–52 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 27 — "With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."

- **Traditional reading:** Jesus' point is that **salvation is entirely God's work**. No one can save themselves by human effort, achievement, or merit. The disciples had just asked, "Who then can be saved?" after Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom. Jesus answers: with men, salvation is impossible — but God can do what man cannot. (Constable, studylight.org)

- **Gill (1746):** Jesus looked on them with an intense gaze, perceiving their anxiety. The statement means God can "reduce a camel to so small a size, as to go through the eye of a needle" — i.e., God can so work on a rich man's heart that he relinquishes trust in riches and enters the kingdom. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-27.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Greek verb ἐμβλέψας (emblepsas) implies an **earnest, intense look**, narrated by an eyewitness (likely Peter). Chrysostom said Jesus looked at them this way to soothe their anxious minds. The sense: a rich man, entangled with wealth, cannot by his own natural strength obtain salvation — it is a supernatural blessing requiring supernatural grace. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-27.htm)

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Salvation is like a camel going through a needle's eye — humanly impossible, but possible with God. Yet God's grace *is* sufficient: the Bible records rich men who were saved (Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea, Barnabas). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** This verse is the foundation for understanding v.45. The radical call to discipleship (drinking Christ's cup, becoming servant of all) is *impossible* for humans — "With men it is impossible, but not with God." The "unless" of v.45 is that the Son of Man must serve *us* day and night for us to follow. (desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-man-came-to-serve)

- **Denominational note:** StudyLight.org records that of 82 commentators on this verse, 34 are classified as Calvinist, 20 Arminian, 13 Dispensational, 2 Lutheran, and 3 Catholic. The verse is much cited in Calvinist–Arminian debates on whether God's enabling grace is resistible.

---

### v. 28 — "Peter began to say to Him, 'Look, we have left everything and followed You.'"

- **Gill:** Peter observed Christ's promise of "treasure in heaven" to the rich young ruler (v.21). He took heart from v.27 — the same power that caused the disciples to leave all could also work on a rich man. Peter's "Lo, we have left all" is both a statement of fact and an implied question: "What shall we have therefore?" (Matthew's version makes this explicit). (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-28.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Mark, possibly writing for Gentile converts, **omits the special promise to the Twelve** that they would "sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/10.htm)

- **Expositor's Greek Testament:** The word ἰδού ("behold/look") betrays Peter's **self-consciousness**, as does the emphatic ἡμεῖς ("we"). In Mark's account, Peter lacks the courage to finish his question, stopping short with the statement of fact. "ἀφήκαμεν" (aorist) refers to a once-for-all act; "ἠκολουθήκαμεν" (perfect) to an abiding condition of following. (biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/mark/10.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Peter's sacrifice was small compared to what Jesus demanded of the rich young ruler, yet they forsook their *all*, whatever it was. Augustine: "St. Peter not only forsook what he had, but also what he desired to have… Peter forsook the whole world, and he received in return the whole world." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-28.htm)

---

### vv. 29–30 — "Truly I tell you… no one who has left home or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for My sake and for the gospel will fail to receive a hundredfold in the present age… along with persecutions — and in the age to come, eternal life."

- **Traditional reading:** Jesus promises abundant recompense both now and eternally. The "hundredfold" is not literal (nobody receives 100 literal mothers), but means the loss is **a hundred times compensated** in value: pardon of sin, peace of conscience, the family of faith, and God's provision. (Barnes, studylight.org)

- **Ellicott:** The phrase **"with persecutions"** is peculiar to Mark. Peter may have remembered this especially because his later experience taught him to see "the fiery trial" as almost the necessary condition of "exceeding joy" (1 Peter 4:12–13). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/10.htm)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The promise of houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children and lands is fulfilled in the **new family of God's people** — the church becomes our family, and what belongs to our brothers and sisters in Christ becomes ours to share. Yet Jesus is realistic: the blessings come *with persecutions*. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Matthew Henry:** "Even when gainers by Christ, let them still expect to suffer for him, till they reach heaven." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-27.htm)

- **Barnes:** "This cannot be taken literally, as promising a hundred times as many mothers, sisters, etc. It means, evidently, that the loss shall be a hundred times compensated… in the possession of religion, we have a hundred times the *value* of all we forsake." God's favour is the security for every blessing. (studylight.org)

---

### v. 31 — "But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first."

- **Traditional reading:** A warning against **mercenary calculation** in discipleship. Peter's implied "what shall we have?" is gently corrected: God's kingdom reverses human rankings. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-31.htm)

- **Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges:** This was "very signally" fulfilled temporarily in Peter himself (his denials), finally in Judas; and wonderfully realised in St. Paul — which is why this passage was chosen as the Gospel reading for the Feast of the Conversion of St. Paul. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-31.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Mark **omits the parable of the Labourers in the Vineyard** (Matthew 20:1–16) that Matthew gives as an illustration of this truth. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/10.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** This weighty sentence corrects any mercenary spirit: first and last are reversed in God's kingdom. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-31.htm)

---

### v. 32 — "As they were going up the road to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking ahead of them. The disciples were amazed, but those who followed were afraid."

- **Constable (studyLight):** Jesus' position **walking ahead** of them, in typical rabbinic fashion, suggests His determination to go to Jerusalem despite His coming death. His resolute attitude probably accounted for the disciples' amazement. Other followers farther behind were afraid because of what Jesus had said lay ahead. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html)

- **The Bible Study New Testament:** The disciples were "filled with alarm" because the Jewish leaders intended to kill Jesus and He was deliberately placing Himself in danger. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ice/mark-10.html)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Jesus' determination to go toward Jerusalem — despite knowing what awaited Him — amazed the disciples. It takes courage to walk into danger willingly. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

---

### vv. 33–34 — "Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles, who will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again."

- **Constable:** This is the **third and most detailed passion prediction**. Each time Jesus gave more information. The first time the disciples reacted violently (Mark 8:32); the second time they did not understand and were afraid to ask (Mark 9:32); this time Mark records no reaction except that an argument about greatness followed immediately — showing they still did not comprehend. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html)

- **Constable provides a chart** showing the remarkable correspondence between the third prediction's six elements (handing over to Sanhedrin, condemnation, handing over to Romans, mocking/spitting/scourging, execution, resurrection) and their fulfillment in the passion narrative. Some critical scholars argue Jesus could not have predicted this, but Constable notes that even without divine foresight, Jesus knew the religious leaders' antagonism and understood Old Testament prophecies of Messiah's suffering (Psalm 22:6–8; Isaiah 50:6; 52:13–53:12). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html)

- **Guzik:** This is the first time Jesus explicitly mentions the **Gentiles' role** (mock, spit, flog, kill). Previously He spoke generally of rejection and death; now details are filled in. Yet the promise of resurrection on the third day is also clearer. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Precept Austin:** This is the last passion prediction as Jesus nears Jerusalem. Knowing time is short, Jesus sets about teaching and modelling kingdom truths. The prediction is part of a larger section (Mark 10:32–52) that pairs the prediction with two responses: the disciples' ambition (vv.35–45) and Bartimaeus' faith (vv.46–52). (preceptaustin.org/mark-10-commentary)

---

### vv. 35–37 — James and John request seats at Jesus' right and left in His glory.

- **Traditional reading:** The request shows **staggering ambition and misunderstanding**. Immediately after Jesus predicts His humiliation and death, James and John ask for the highest positions of honour. The person at a ruler's right hand held the highest assigned position, the left the second highest. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html)

- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** "What they wanted from Jesus was status. What they wanted from Jesus was to be placed in a position of power." They asked for the penultimate and next-highest positions in the kingdom. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-kingdom-climbers)

- **Matthew's parallel:** Matthew 20:20 notes that their mother Salome (likely Jesus' aunt) voiced the request. Mark puts the words in James and John's mouths because they came from their hearts. They may have thought their **family connection** (they were Jesus' cousins) justified the request. (Constable, studylight.org)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Here, again, the disciples show their utter ignorance of the prophecies, and of their Master's kingdom." They seem to have thought Jesus' resurrection meant His taking possession of a great empire, so they asked for the chief posts. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-35.htm)

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** James and John got one thing right — that Jesus was destined for glory ("in Your glory"). They got almost everything else wrong. "They probably didn't understand the cup and the baptism that Jesus was talking about." (desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-man-came-to-serve)

---

### v. 38 — "You do not know what you are asking… Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?"

- **John Piper:** The **cup** = the death Jesus was about to endure (cf. Mark 14:36, "remove this cup from Me"). The **baptism** = an immersion in suffering (cf. Luke 12:50, "I have a baptism to undergo"). Jesus' pathway to glory is through suffering and death. (desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-man-came-to-serve)

- **Guzik:** Jesus did not rebuke their ambition but **redirected it**. Greatness in the kingdom is possible, but the path is suffering. The cup is the cup of God's wrath that Jesus would drink on the cross; the baptism is being overwhelmed by suffering. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Ye know not that ye are asking for sufferings, which must needs pave the way to glory." The cup = inward sufferings; the baptism = outward sufferings. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/10-35.htm)

---

### v. 39 — "We can," they answered. "You will drink the cup that I drink," Jesus said, "and you will be baptized with the baptism that I undergo."

- **Traditional reading:** James and John answered boldly but **naively**. Jesus prophesies they *will* indeed share in His sufferings: James became the first apostolic martyr (Acts 12:2), and John endured exile and persecution.

- **Guzik:** Jesus did not dismiss their ambition as impossible. "He told them they would indeed share in His suffering, but the places of honour were not His to dispense arbitrarily." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

---

### v. 40 — "But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared."

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** Jesus does not say the Father has not *revealed* this to Him; He says it is "not Mine to give." Piper suggests: "I and the Father have tugs of affection that we often do not gratify in immediate ways. Instead we submit them to the guidance of infinite wisdom." The Father's preparations are always better. The answer "No, that is not mine to give" always means "My Father has prepared something better. Trust him." (desiringgod.org/articles/a-prayer-jesus-would-not-answer)

- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** The Father will determine who sits at Jesus' right and left. This is a corrective: even Jesus, in His incarnate state, submits to the Father's sovereign determination. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-kingdom-climbers)

---

### v. 41 — "When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John."

- **Traditional reading:** The indignation was likely not righteous anger at the brothers' presumption, but **jealousy** — they were upset because James and John got there first. The ten were no less ambitious; they were simply outmanoeuvred.

- **Guzik:** "The other disciples were probably indignant not because James and John asked for something wrong, but because they wanted those positions themselves." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

---

### vv. 42–44 — Jesus teaches that greatness comes through servanthood and slavery.

- **Traditional reading:** Jesus contrasts the world's leadership model ("lord it over them") with the kingdom model: **greatness = service, first = slave of all**. In Roman society, rulers exercised absolute authority; in Christ's community, authority is expressed through servanthood.

- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** "It shall not be so among you" — Jesus establishes a completely different ethos for His community. The world's hierarchy is inverted. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-kingdom-climbers)

- **Guzik:** The word for "servant" (διάκονος) and "slave" (δοῦλος) are significant. A *diakonos* serves willingly; a *doulos* is a bond-slave, owned by another. Jesus calls His followers not merely to volunteer service but to **total surrender** of rights. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

---

### v. 45 — "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many."

- **John Piper (Desiring God):** This is the **great Christmas text** in Mark. Jesus does not merely come as a teacher calling for sacrificial discipleship — "He comes to do two things: One, to give his life as a ransom for many. And he comes, secondly, to serve his disciples." Piper stresses: "the good news of Christmas is that the radical call to Christian discipleship is NOT a call to serve Jesus, but to be *served* by Jesus as we serve others, and to be ransomed by him from death." The "for" (γάρ) connects back: the reason we serve is because the Son of Man first serves us. (desiringgod.org/messages/the-son-of-man-came-to-serve)

- **Guzik:** "Ransom" (λύτρον) was the price paid to free a slave or prisoner. "For many" — a Semitic expression meaning "for all," but with the sense of the many who believe. The ransom was substitutionary: Jesus gave His life *in place of* the many. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Traditional atonement theology:** This verse is a key **proof-text for substitutionary atonement** across all major Protestant traditions (Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal). All affirm Christ's death as a ransom paid to liberate sinners from bondage to sin and death. Differences exist on the precise nature of the transaction (to whom the ransom was paid, the extent of the atonement), but all traditions found here teach that Christ's death was a substitutionary, liberating payment.

---

### v. 46 — "Next, they came to Jericho. And as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting beside the road."

- **R.C. Sproul (Ligonier):** Bartimaeus is **the only person Jesus healed who is named in the Synoptic Gospels**. Mark explains "Bartimaeus" means "son of Timaeus" — a redundancy for Jewish readers, suggesting Mark wrote for Gentiles unfamiliar with Aramaic naming conventions. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-son-man-servant)

- **Ligonier devotional:** "Bartimaeus' name means 'son of Timaeus,' Mark's note of the name's meaning is unnecessary — unless he is writing for a Gentile audience who does not know Jewish naming conventions. Thus, we have further evidence that Mark's intended audience consists mainly of Gentiles." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blind-bartimaeus)

- **Setting:** NT Jericho was about 17–18 miles north of Jerusalem, an oasis city along the merchant roads — ideal for a beggar. Sproul notes it was an ancient city, one of the longest continuously inhabited in the world alongside Damascus. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-son-man-servant)

- **Matthew's Gospel** mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30); Mark and Luke focus on the spokesman, Bartimaeus. (Constable/Ligonier)

---

### vv. 47–48 — Bartimaeus cries out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" The crowd rebukes him, but he cries all the louder.

- **Ligonier devotional:** "Bartimaeus calls out to Jesus for mercy, calling Him 'Son of David'… This shows remarkable **messianic insight** on Bartimaeus' part, for 'Son of David' is a title for the Messiah and Jesus has not been openly revealing His messianic identity (see Mark 8:27–30)." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blind-bartimaeus)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** "Son of David" was a recognised messianic title. Bartimaeus "knew who Jesus was better than most of the religious leaders of his day." When the crowd tried to silence him, he "cried out all the more" — persistence in faith. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Spurgeon's sermon outline** (referenced on biblehub.com) highlights Bartimaeus' faith's "quickness in grasping the gracious opportunity" and how "whilst it cries and begs." (biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/the_blind_beggar.htm)

- **R.C. Sproul:** The crowd represents those who would hinder people from coming to Jesus. Bartimaeus' persistence in crying louder is an example of **faith that will not be silenced**. (learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-son-man-servant)

---

### vv. 49–50 — Jesus stops and calls him. Bartimaeus throws off his cloak and comes.

- **Traditional reading:** Jesus "stopped" — on His determined journey toward the cross, the cry of one blind beggar halts the Son of God. This demonstrates Jesus' compassion and the value He places on individual faith.

- **Spurgeon** (from sermon outline): "Observe how eagerly [faith] obeyed the call." Bartimaeus threw aside his garment — likely his only possession of value and what he used to collect alms — "he rose and came to Jesus." (biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/the_blind_beggar.htm)

- **Guzik:** "Throwing off his cloak" was significant: a blind beggar's cloak was his most important possession. By casting it aside, Bartimaeus demonstrated **faith that Jesus would heal him** — he wouldn't need the beggar's cloak anymore. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

---

### v. 51 — "What do you want Me to do for you?" Jesus asked. 'Rabboni,' said the blind man, 'let me see again.'"

- **Guzik:** Jesus asks the **same question** He asked James and John in v.36: "What do you want Me to do for you?" James and John asked for status and glory; Bartimaeus asked for mercy and sight. The contrast is intentional: the blind man sees who Jesus really is, while the seeing disciples are spiritually blind. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Ligonier devotional:** "What sets Bartimaeus apart as one who exemplifies true discipleship is his request for the restoration of his sight, not special favor in God's kingdom." Bartimaeus does not seek privilege; his cry for mercy shows awareness that healing is **undeserved**. "He is the picture of the true disciple of Christ, the one who knows that he relies only on grace." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blind-bartimaeus)

- **"Rabboni"** is an intensified form of "Rabbi," meaning "my great/master teacher." It conveys deep personal reverence.

---

### v. 52 — "'Go,' said Jesus, 'your faith has healed you.' And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road."

- **Traditional reading:** The Greek verb σέσωκέν (sesōken, "has healed/saved you") can mean both physical healing and spiritual salvation. Bartimaeus' faith was the instrument through which he received both.

- **Ligonier (R.C. Sproul):** "As soon as Bartimaeus received his sight, he saw Jesus, and he wanted nothing more than to **follow Him to Jerusalem**. That is the desire of all who are given eyes to see and ears to hear the truth of the gospel of Jesus Christ." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blind-bartimaeus)

- **Guzik:** Bartimaeus "followed Jesus along the road" — the road to Jerusalem, toward the cross. "He didn't just receive his sight and go his own way; he became a disciple. His faith was not just for healing but for following." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-10/)

- **Literary structure note (Constable via Precept Austin):** Mark frames the entire journey section (8:22–10:52) with two healings of blind men — the gradual healing at Bethsaida (8:22–26) and Bartimaeus (10:46–52). The journey is "dominated by Jesus' urgent efforts to deal with the disciples' blindness to the things of God." Bartimaeus, the blind man who *sees*, is the model disciple. (preceptaustin.org/mark-10-commentary)

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

### On v.27 and v.45 — Calvinist vs. Arminian

StudyLight.org records that v.27 is a frequent point of reference in the Calvinist–Arminian debate, with 34 Calvinist and 20 Arminian commentators addressing it. The Calvinist reading (e.g., Gill) stresses God's sovereign, effectual grace to overcome human impossibility; the Arminian reading (e.g., Contending for the Faith, 2022) stresses God's enabling grace which may be resisted. Both traditions agree salvation is impossible by human effort alone.

### On v.45 — "Ransom for Many" and Extent of the Atonement

- **Reformed / Particular Baptist:** "Many" means the elect — Christ's ransom was definite and effectual for those whom the Father gave Him. The ransom actually secures salvation, not merely makes it possible.
- **Lutheran and Methodist/Arminian:** "Many" means all humanity — Christ's ransom is universal in extent, sufficient for all, but applied only to those who believe.

Both views affirm substitutionary atonement (Christ dying in the sinner's place) as the core meaning of "ransom."

### On v.52 — "Your faith has healed you" and Prosperity/Word of Faith teaching

The pages consulted (enduringword.com, ligonier.org, desiringgod.org, biblehub.com) do not directly address prosperity-gospel interpretations of this verse. The traditional reading from all consulted sources uniformly treats Bartimaeus' healing as an act of divine mercy grounded in grace, received by faith, resulting in discipleship — not as a "formula" for guaranteed physical healing.

### On vv.29–30 — "Hundredfold now in this time" and Prosperity teaching

None of the consulted pages explicitly refute prosperity interpretations, but Barnes (Presbyterian) and Henry (Puritan) are careful to interpret the "hundredfold" **non-literally** — as spiritual compensation and the blessings of the family of faith, not a literal multiplication of material wealth. Henry adds: "Let us learn contentment in a low state, and to watch against the love of riches in a high one."

### Catholic and Orthodox readings

The searches did not return specific pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org on this passage within the search limits. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican-leaning) and the references to Chrysostom (via biblehub.com) represent the patristic reading that the Greek fathers shared with both East and West: the emphasis falls on God's grace enabling what is humanly impossible, and on Bartimaeus as a model of humble, persistent faith. The Catholic Haydock Commentary is listed on biblehub.com but its specific content on these verses was not fetched within limits.

### Modern critical scholarship

- **Constable (studyLight) notes** that some modern scholars (e.g., Nineham) argue Jesus could not have predicted his passion in such detail, suggesting the predictions are *vaticinia ex eventu* (prophecies written after the fact). Constable responds that even without supernatural foreknowledge, Jesus could have anticipated what awaited Him from His knowledge of the Old Testament and the religious leaders' hostility. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-10.html)
